## The data science cycle

:::: cols
::: {}
Every project in this course goes round this cycle, from HW1 to your group project.

- **Exploration and analysis** go round and round: look, test, look again.
- To answer more, go back: **fetch more data**, or **refine the question**, and round again.
- **Reproducible** applies to every step.
- Your report follows the cycle, and ends with *How to reproduce*.
:::
::: {}
```{=html}
{{< include ../../public/img/introduction/diagram-cycle.svg >}}
```
<p class="small muted">After the cycle in Wickham, Çetinkaya-Rundel &amp; Grolemund, <i>R for Data Science</i> (2e).</p>
:::
::::

::: notes
Keep this slide in mind: every project that follows is told along this cycle.
:::

## Course aims

<p class="big">From a question to an answer anyone can check.</p>

<p class="muted">You will write code, but code is not the point. The science is.</p>

::: {.twocol .aims}
- Turn a vague question into one that **data can answer**, and choose methods that fit it.
- **Find, collect and combine** data from files, databases, APIs and the web.
- **Clean, explore and visualise** data, and see when a pattern might mislead.
- Draw conclusions the evidence supports, with their **uncertainty and limitations**.
- Make every analysis **reproducible**: Git and GitHub, a clear README, a workflow others can run.
- Work in a **team** on shared code: branches, pull requests, code review.
- **Communicate** results honestly, clearly and usefully.
:::

<p class="more">More: <a href="../../about#what-you-ll-be-able-to-do">Course information</a></p>

::: notes
One aim per step of the cycle, plus working together and telling others. The three projects
that follow show what this looks like at three levels of ambition.
:::

# Are baby names a fashion? {.divider}

<p class="muted">Small project · one source</p>

## Aim {data-project="Baby names"}

<p class="lead">Are baby names a fashion: do they come and go, and come back?</p>

:::: cols
::: {}
- A fashion is popular, then forgotten, then popular again.
- Parents often name children after grandparents or great-grandparents. If names are a fashion, a name should **come back after about three generations**.
:::
::: {.fragment}
**What we need to find out**

- How common each name was, **every year for 100 years**.
- Which names were common, then rare, then common again.
- What the data can and **cannot** tell us.
:::
::::

::: notes
Before anything is done: what are we trying to find out, and what would count as an answer?
:::

## Overview {data-project="Baby names"}

::: workflow
<div><span class="kicker">Data</span><b>Statistics Sweden (SCB)</b>
<ul><li>downloaded straight from their database by a short script</li><li>how many people born each year 1922–2021 have each of the 200 most common names</li></ul></div>
<div><span class="kicker">Cleaning</span><b>A tidy table</b>
<ul><li>reshape the table so it is easy to work with</li><li>handle the gaps: SCB hides very small numbers</li><li>turn counts into shares, so years can be compared</li></ul></div>
<div><span class="kicker">Analysis</span><b>Find the comebacks</b>
<ul><li>plot each name over 100 years</li><li>a comeback score: common in 1922–35, rare in 1960–80, common again in 2005–21</li></ul></div>
<div class="result"><span class="kicker">Results</span><b>Yes, with a catch</b>
<ul><li>Ella, Elsa, Alice, Astrid, Ebba top the score</li><li>the top 10 names: 59% of those counted for 1922, 24% for 2021</li><li>only the living are counted</li></ul></div>
:::

<p class="wfcode"><code>names/fetch.py</code> → <code>names/data/</code> → <code>names/report.qmd</code> → <code>report.md</code><span>one command: <code>uv run quarto render</code></span></p>

::: notes
The whole project in one slide: where the data came from, what we did to it, what we found.
The next slides show the result and the catch.
:::

## Measures {data-project="Baby names"}

::: {.defs .two}
<div><b>Share of a birth year</b><p>How common a name is among the babies born in one year.</p><p class="muted">People born that year with the name, divided by everyone born that year with one of the 200 names in the table. A share, not a count, so years with many or few births can be compared.</p></div>
<div><b>Comeback score</b><p>How well a name fits "common, then rare, then common again".</p><p class="muted">Its share in 1922–35 divided by its share in 1960–80, and its share in 2005–21 divided by its share in 1960–80; the score is the smaller of the two. High only if the name was common both before and after the dip.</p></div>
:::

::: notes
Two numbers, defined before any graph. The comeback score takes the smaller ratio, so a name has
to be common on both sides of the dip to score high.
:::

## Results {data-project="Baby names"}

<p class="lead">Names skip three generations.</p>

<img src="../../img/introduction/names-comebacks.svg" alt="Share of births named Elsa, Alice and Astrid, 1922–2021: high in the 1920s, almost zero in 1960–80, high again after 2000">

<p class="small">Share of each birth year with the name, among the 200 most common names in Sweden. Data: SCB.</p>

::: notes
Common in the 1920s, nearly gone around 1970 (grey band), back after 2000. Ask: who in the room
has a grandmother or great-grandmother called Elsa, Alice or Astrid?
:::

## Limitations {data-project="Baby names"}

<p class="lead">The table only shows people alive today, with names common today.</p>

::: {.defs .two .lim}
<div><b>Only the living are counted</b><p>SCB counts people <b>alive in Sweden in 2021</b>, by year of birth. The dead and the emigrated are gone.</p><p class="muted">Born 1922: only <b>1,543</b> people left in the table. Born 1970: <b>82,020</b>. The 1920s shares rest on few people, and SCB hides counts under 10.</p></div>
<div><b>Only names common today</b><p>The 200 names are the most common in Sweden <b>today</b>. A 1920s name that never came back is not in the list.</p><p class="muted">For 1922, only <b>44</b> of the 200 names are visible. Fashions that died for good can't be seen, so the data <b>favours finding comebacks</b>.</p></div>
<div><b>Shares of 200 names, not of all babies</b><p>A share is out of the people with one of these 200 names, not out of everyone born that year.</p><p class="muted">For 2021 the table has <b>26,599</b> people: most babies today have names outside the list.</p></div>
<div><b>Our choice of periods</b><p>The score uses 1922–35, 1960–80 and 2005–21: our choice.</p><p class="muted">Checked: moving the cut-offs by about five years keeps <b>9–10</b> of the same top ten. This one matters little.</p></div>
:::

<p class="small" style="margin-top:.8em">So: these names really did come back, but the data can't tell us how common comebacks are, or <b>why</b> names come back.</p>

::: notes
Survivorship bias is the big one: the table is a picture of who is alive today, so it can show
names that came back but not names that disappeared. The cut-off check is an example of testing
your own choice and reporting that it holds.
:::

# Why does electricity cost more in Malmö than in Luleå? {.divider}

<p class="muted">Medium project · two sources combined</p>

## Aim {data-project="Electricity prices"}

<p class="lead">How much more does the south pay for electricity, and is the weather the reason?</p>

:::: cols
::: {}
- Electricity in Malmö usually costs more than in Luleå, although it is the same country and the same market.
- One explanation: when there is **little wind** in the south, power has to come from the north, and the grid can't carry enough.
:::
::: {.fragment}
**What we need to find out**

- How big the **gap** between Malmö and Luleå is, day by day.
- Whether the gap is **bigger on calm days** than on windy days.
- **How sure** we can be, and **how much** of the gap the weather explains.
:::
::::

::: notes
The question and what would answer it, before any data. The next slide is the background
needed to follow it: the four price zones.
:::

## Background {data-project="Electricity prices"}

<p class="lead">Four zones, one country.</p>

:::: cols
::: {}
- Since 2011 Sweden has **four price zones**, SE1 in the north to SE4 in the south.
- Much of the power is produced in the north, much of it used in the south.
- When the grid can't carry enough south, the prices split.
:::
::: {}
```{=html}
{{< include ../../public/img/introduction/diagram-zones.svg >}}
```
<p class="small muted">Mean spot price 2023–2025. Data: Nord Pool via elprisetjustnu.se.</p>
:::
::::

## Overview {data-project="Electricity prices"}

::: workflow
<div><span class="kicker">Data</span><b>Two free online sources</b>
<ul><li>electricity prices for the four zones, every hour (every 15 minutes from October 2025), 2023–2025</li><li>SMHI: wind and temperature in Malmö</li><li>downloaded by a script and saved, so anyone can rerun it</li></ul></div>
<div><span class="kicker">Cleaning</span><b>One row per day</b>
<ul><li>one price per zone and day</li><li>watch out for clock changes</li><li>put prices and weather side by side: 1,074 days</li></ul></div>
<div><span class="kicker">Analysis</span><b>Does wind matter?</b>
<ul><li>the gap: Malmö minus Luleå, each day</li><li>compare calm days with windy days</li><li>how sure can we be, and how much does weather explain?</li></ul></div>
<div class="result"><span class="kicker">Results</span><b>Partly</b>
<ul><li>Malmö 0.66, Luleå 0.31 kr/kWh on average</li><li>on calm days the gap is 0.40 kr/kWh bigger: not chance</li><li>but weather explains only about a fifth of it</li></ul></div>
:::

<p class="wfcode"><code>electricity/fetch_prices.py + fetch_weather.py</code> → <code>electricity/data/</code> → <code>electricity/report.qmd</code> → <code>report.md</code><span>one command: <code>uv run quarto render</code></span></p>

::: notes
Two sources, put side by side by date. The cleaning is where the work was; the next slide shows it.
:::

## Data cleaning {data-project="Electricity prices"}

<p class="lead">Where the work was.</p>

```{=html}
{{< include ../../public/img/introduction/diagram-cleaning.svg >}}
```

::: twocol
- Prices came **every hour**, then from October 2025 **every 15 minutes**: a simple average counts them wrongly.
- Clocks change twice a year: some days have **23 or 25 hours**.
- Prices use world time, the weather Swedish dates: match them to the **right** day.
- **22 days** have no weather: dropped, and reported.
:::

::: notes
Each bullet, done wrong, would shift the result without any error. The report shows every step in code.
:::

## Measures {data-project="Electricity prices"}

::: {.defs .four}
<div><b>Daily price</b><p>What electricity cost in a zone on one day.</p><p class="muted">The average of the hourly (later 15-minute) prices, each weighted by how long it lasted. In kr/kWh.</p></div>
<div><b>The gap</b><p>How much more Malmö paid than Luleå.</p><p class="muted">Malmö's (SE4) daily price minus Luleå's (SE1), for each day. Positive: the south paid more.</p></div>
<div><b>Wind quarters</b><p>Calm days compared with windy days.</p><p class="muted">Sort the days by the wind in Malmö and split them into four equal groups, from the calmest quarter to the windiest.</p></div>
<div><b>Share explained</b><p>How much of the gap goes with the weather.</p><p class="muted">Fit a straight line of the gap on wind and temperature: the share of the day-to-day ups and downs the line accounts for (R²).</p></div>
:::

::: notes
Four numbers, defined before any graph: the next slides use each of them.
:::

## Exploration {data-project="Electricity prices"}

<p class="lead">The gap, month by month.</p>

<img src="../../img/introduction/electricity-zones.svg" alt="Monthly mean spot price in SE4 Malmö and SE1 Luleå, 2023–2025; Malmö is above Luleå almost every month">

<p class="small">The shaded area is the gap. Is it the wind? Wind power in the south should push southern prices down.</p>

::: notes
The gap is the shaded area. Question: how big is it, and does it go with the weather?
:::

## Results {data-project="Electricity prices"}

<p class="lead">Calm days, big gap.</p>

<img src="../../img/introduction/electricity-wind.svg" alt="Mean price gap by wind quarter: 0.55 SEK per kWh on the calmest days, falling to 0.15 on the windiest">

On the calmest quarter of days the gap is **0.40 kr/kWh bigger** than on the windiest quarter, far more than chance would give. But wind and temperature explain only **18%** of the day-to-day gap.

::: notes
"Not chance" comes from a bootstrap interval (0.34–0.47), which you will see in the second half. The 18%: the rest is the
grid, nuclear maintenance and continental prices, which this data doesn't contain.
Correlation, not cause: windy days also differ in season and demand.
:::

# Is AI a bubble? {.divider}

<p class="muted">Ambitious project · three sources, and a question that needs work first</p>

## Aim {data-project="AI bubble"}

<p class="lead">Many say AI shares are in a bubble. What can data say about that?</p>

:::: cols
::: {}
- In a **bubble**, prices rise far above what things are worth, until they crash. 1929 and the dot-com boom of 2000 are famous examples.
- But "bubble" can't be **observed directly**, and whether it bursts is a **prediction**.
:::
::: {.fragment}
**What we need to find out**

- Which **measurable signs** people mean when they say "bubble".
- How unusual **today** is on each sign, compared with **1929, 2000 and the crypto boom**.
- What the data **can't** answer.
:::
::::

::: notes
The hard part comes first here: the question has to be made measurable before any data is fetched.
:::

## Research question {data-project="AI bubble"}

<p class="lead">From a vague question to three signs we can measure.</p>

```{=html}
{{< include ../../public/img/introduction/diagram-operationalise.svg >}}
```

::: notes
Deciding what to measure is the hard part of this project. The next slide says what each sign is.
:::

## Measures {data-project="AI bubble"}

::: defs
<div><b>Valuations</b><p>How expensive shares are compared with what the companies earn.</p><p class="muted">US share prices divided by the average earnings of the last 10 years (Shiller's "CAPE"). 40 means paying 40 kr for every 1 kr of yearly profit.</p></div>
<div><b>Price growth</b><p>How fast prices have risen.</p><p class="muted">The NASDAQ tech index today divided by its value 5 years earlier. ×2 means prices doubled in 5 years.</p></div>
<div><b>Attention</b><p>How much people talk about it.</p><p class="muted">The share of Hacker News headlines (a tech forum) that mention AI, compared with bitcoin and crypto earlier.</p></div>
:::

<p style="margin-top:1em">For each: how does <b>today</b> compare with every month before, and with <b>1929, 2000 and crypto</b>?</p>

::: notes
Make sure everyone knows what each number means before we look at any results.
:::

## Overview {data-project="AI bubble"}

::: workflow
<div><span class="kicker">Data</span><b>Three sources</b>
<ul><li>share prices vs company earnings, every month since 1871</li><li>the NASDAQ tech index since 1971</li><li>4.8 million headlines from Hacker News, a tech forum</li></ul></div>
<div><span class="kicker">Cleaning</span><b>Months, comparable</b>
<ul><li>line the three sources up month by month</li><li>read the dates carefully: one source writes October oddly</li><li>use shares of all headlines, not raw counts</li></ul></div>
<div><span class="kicker">Analysis</span><b>How unusual is today?</b>
<ul><li>each sign against its own history</li><li>how unusual is today, compared with every month before?</li><li>compare with 1929, 2000 and crypto</li></ul></div>
<div class="result"><span class="kicker">Results</span><b>Two of three signs</b>
<ul><li>valuations: higher than almost every month since 1871</li><li>attention: AI is in 14% of headlines; bitcoin peaked at 3%</li><li>price growth: ordinary (×1.6 in 5 years)</li></ul></div>
:::

<p class="wfcode"><code>ai-bubble/fetch.py</code> → <code>ai-bubble/data/</code> → <code>ai-bubble/report.qmd</code> → <code>report.md</code><span>one command: <code>uv run quarto render</code></span></p>

::: notes
The whole project in one slide. Next: the three signs, one at a time.
:::

## Results: valuations {data-project="AI bubble"}

<p class="lead">Second only to 2000.</p>

<img src="../../img/introduction/ai-cape.svg" alt="Cyclically adjusted price-earnings ratio of US stocks since 1881, with 1929, 2000 and today marked; today is above 1929 and just below 2000">

<p class="small"><b>Valuations:</b> US share prices divided by ten years of company earnings (Shiller's "CAPE"). Higher means more expensive. Data: Robert Shiller.</p>

::: notes
Only the months around the 2000 peak were higher. 1929 was lower than today.
A cleaning trap: Shiller writes October as 2026.1, which as a number is the same as January.
:::

## Results: price growth {data-project="AI bubble"}

<p class="lead">An ordinary pace.</p>

<img src="../../img/introduction/ai-nasdaq.svg" alt="NASDAQ divided by its value five years earlier, since 1976; the 2000 peak is far higher than today">

<p class="small"><b>Price growth:</b> the NASDAQ index divided by its value five years earlier. ×2 means prices doubled. Data: FRED.</p>

<p>Today ×1.6: higher than only <b>40%</b> of months. In 2000: ×5.9. <span class="accent">This sign is missing.</span></p>

::: notes
Report the evidence that goes against your story too.
:::

## Results: attention {data-project="AI bubble"}

<p class="lead">Four times bitcoin's peak.</p>

<img src="../../img/introduction/ai-attention.svg" alt="Share of Hacker News story titles mentioning AI, bitcoin and crypto, 2007 to today; AI is far above the earlier crypto peaks">

<p class="small"><b>Attention:</b> the share of Hacker News headlines with each word. Data: Hacker News.</p>

## Conclusions and limitations {data-project="AI bubble"}

::: scorecard
<div class="yes"><span class="tick">✓</span><b>Valuations</b><span class="num">40.7</span><span class="muted">price vs earnings today · 44.2 in 2000</span></div>
<div class="yes"><span class="tick">✓</span><b>Attention</b><span class="num">14 %</span><span class="muted">of HN titles · bitcoin's peak: 3 %</span></div>
<div class="no"><span class="tick">✗</span><b>Price growth</b><span class="num">×1.6</span><span class="muted">in 5 years · ×5.9 in 2000</span></div>
:::

<p class="big" style="margin-top:.8em">Two of three signs are there. Whether a crash follows is <span class="accent">not in the data</span>.</p>

- High valuations can last for years; if AI raises earnings as expected, prices may be right.
- Three signs is our choice. US data, an English-language forum, few past bubbles to compare with.

::: notes
What makes this project ambitious: a hard question, results checked against history, and
conclusions that state what can't be concluded.
:::

## Grading

Each assignment is scored **0–100**, and **65** passes. A late hand-in costs **30 points**:

::: scale
<div class="track"><div class="fail"></div><div class="pass"></div></div>
<div class="tick" style="left:0%">0</div><div class="tick pass-tick" style="left:65%">65 pass</div><div class="tick" style="left:100%">100</div>
<div class="marker" style="left:80%">80</div>
<div class="marker late" style="left:50%">late: 80 − 30 = 50, not passed</div>
:::

::: rules
<div><b>Peer review is required</b>review a classmate by Thursday 23:59</div>
<div><b>Improve until Friday</b>the Friday 23:59 version is graded</div>
<div class="hot"><b>Late: −30</b>and no peer review</div>
<div class="hot"><b>Final deadline <span data-course="finalDeadline">Fri 15 Jan, 23:59</span></b>miss it and you redo all assignments next year</div>
:::

## Hand-in

```{=html}
{{< include ../../public/img/introduction/diagram-handin.svg >}}
```

- **The check** renders your report on a clean computer. Green means anyone can get your numbers.
- Push again to the same branch and the pull request updates; the check runs again.
- One repository for all five assignments: <code>&lt;username&gt;-assignments</code>. You'll get an invite.

<p class="more">More: <a href="../../guide">How we work</a></p>

::: notes
We'll go through this in detail in the second half. The check is the reproducibility test:
green means anyone can get your numbers.
:::

::: milestones
<div><span class="when">Now</span><b>Form a group</b>2–3 people, a question of your own</div>

<div><span class="when">Nov – Jan</span><b>The full cycle</b>reproducible, with pull requests</div>
<div><span class="when" data-course="project">Fri 8 Jan, 23:59</span><b>Hand in</b>report about as long as an assignment</div>
<div><span class="when" data-course="presentation">Mon 11 Jan, 13:00–16:00</span><b>Present</b>15–20 minutes per group</div>
:::

- **The proposal** names the group, the question and its data, and the grade you aim for. We check that the scope fits that grade.
- Same tools as the assignments: one repository per group, branches, pull requests, the check.
- Attending the presentations is compulsory.

<p style="margin-top:.6em">Use the three projects you just saw as reference points for scope.</p>
